newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU drive to freer grain markets stirs controversy.
newsitem.headline: EU drive to freer grain markets stirs controversy.

text.p: European Union efforts to retain its share of an expanding world grain market by making its farmers more competitive provoked conflicting reactions on Thursday from leading member states.

At a two-day grain conference, Britain showed the greatest enthusiasm for further radical, market-oriented reforms and Germany the least with France standing in the middle wanting to maximise exports while protecting poorer farmers.

"The part which can be played by export refunds or production-linked subsidies seems destined to fall," said David Roberts, European Commission deputy director general for agriculture, sparking off heated reactions.
The EU's planned expansion eastwards and further freeing of world farm trade after 2000 is seen forcing further changes following far-reaching reforms agreed in 1992.
The EU is the world's second major grain exporter with 14 percent of the market but trails far behind the 46 percent share held by the United States.
World grain demand is expected to grow steadily, especially in south east Asia, as a result of population growth and rising incomes in key countries.
A senior British agricultural official, Kate Timms, said there was a pressing need for further EU cereals reforms.

"Set-aside, export subsidies and intervention will not be sustainable in the long run... Nor are they readily compatible with the larger EU production capacity which will follow EU enlargement," Timms said.

Farm support prices should be cut until export subsidies become unnecessary, aid to farmers based on the area cultivated phased out and payments for setting aside farmland abolished, according to the British view.
The pain for farmers would be eased by the payment of temporary aid to help them adjust to the new conditions.

But Germany strongly believes that EU farmers should continue to be subsidised as long as domestic prices remained higher than world levels. Farmers should also continue to be compensated for price cuts made under the 1992 reforms.
It also much prefers production controls to pricing mechanisms.
"Supply control through land set-aside is an effective instrument," Herman Engelhardt, head of the German agriculture ministry's cereals division, told the conference.
"No instrument embedded in it (1992 EU farm reform) is superfluous," he added.
But France, the Union's main grain exporter, urged it to wind down the cumbersome set-aside system so as to maximise output and exports.
"The EU can rediscover its role as a major exporter," said Francois de la Gueronniere, of the French agriculture ministry, pointing to this year's record grain harvest.
But he cautioned against radical reforms, urging instead a gradual approach taking account of farmers' social, economic and financial needs.
The United States, which recently set a pointer towards freer and more competitive future farm trade, warned that it would not surrender any market share.
"These (EU) reforms will...change the competitive balance and will undoubtedly result in compensating adjustments by Europe's competitors," said George Pope, U.S. agricultural attache in Brussels.
